title: Connecting On-Premises to Azure
description: Choose between VPN and ExpressRoute for a hybrid workload that must reach a legacy database.

data.text: A new Azure-hosted API must read from an on-premises SQL Server in the company data centre. The data centre connects to the internet through a single 200 Mbps fibre link. Traffic to the API is bursty and the business tolerates a few minutes of degradation but not a full outage. How do you connect the two networks?

Start with a **site-to-site VPN** using a **VPN Gateway** in a dedicated `GatewaySubnet`. It runs over the internet, encrypts traffic with IPsec/IKE, and is provisioned in under an hour. If the workload later becomes business-critical — voice, real-time trading, or a very large data transfer — move to **ExpressRoute** for a private, SLA-backed circuit that bypasses the public internet. Because the on-premises link is a single point of failure, ensure the design has a fallback path.

data.title: Site-to-site VPN gateway (Bicep)

data.text: Regardless of the transport, put the private endpoint on the on-premises database side inside a hub VNet and share it with spokes using **VNet peering**. Application code then talks to a private IP, and no traffic traverses a public endpoint.

ExpressRoute has a multi-week provisioning lead time through a connectivity provider and a substantially higher monthly cost. VPN over the internet is immediate and cheap, and for an internal API reading a database it is usually fast enough. The decision flips when you need guaranteed jitter, a private path for compliance, or bandwidth beyond what the internet link supports.

cards.title: Site-to-site VPN
cons: Latency and jitter depend on the internet
Throughput bounded by your ISP link

cards.title: ExpressRoute
pros: Does not traverse the public internet
